questions.prompt: What is the primary business outcome Project ADB is expected to deliver?

options.text: Replace four legacy servicing systems with one core platform and cut onboarding from nine days to two
Migrate all customer data to a public cloud provider within one quarter
Retire the client's relationship manager network
Build a standalone mobile app with no integration to the core

questions.explanation: The agreed programme objective is consolidation of four legacy systems into a single core platform, reducing new-customer onboarding from nine days to two. The other options are not part of the agreed scope.

questions.prompt: In ADB terminology, what does 'origination' refer to?

options.text: The nightly reconciliation between the ledger and the core host
The journey that creates a new customer record and product holding
A post-sale change to an existing customer record
The process of archiving closed accounts

questions.explanation: Origination is the new-business journey — it creates the customer record and the product holding. Post-sale changes are servicing, not origination.

questions.prompt: Who owns the decision on data, access and environment readiness?

options.text: The HCLTech engineering lead
The client product owner
The Meridian delivery lead
The learning program manager

questions.explanation: The Meridian delivery lead owns data, access and environment readiness. The product owner owns scope and acceptance, while the HCLTech engineering lead owns technical standards and quality gates.

questions.prompt: A question about a business term is blocking your task. What is the expected first step?

options.text: Make a reasonable assumption and continue quietly
Raise it in the shared project channel so the answer is searchable
Wait for the next weekly sync to raise it
Email the client directly

questions.explanation: Domain questions belong in the shared project channel, where the answer is searchable and reusable by the next joiner. Do not block on the weekly sync, and never assume silently.

questions.prompt: Which stakeholder group owns backlog prioritisation?

options.text: The client product owner
The QA squad
The learning program manager
The release manager

questions.explanation: The client product owner owns scope and therefore backlog prioritisation. The QA squad owns regression execution and the release manager coordinates the release cut.

questions.prompt: How is access provisioned on this project?

options.text: By individual request for each system you need
By role-based bundle, matched to your learning role
Automatically on your first login, for all environments
By asking a teammate to share their credentials

questions.explanation: Access is granted as a bundle matched to your learning role (developer, tester or lead). Individual per-system requests and credential sharing are both prohibited.

questions.prompt: What is the correct response to a certificate trust error on the internal registry?

options.text: Disable TLS verification for the registry
Re-import the corporate root certificate and restart the terminal
Add the registry to your browser exceptions
Clone the repository over a personal hotspot instead

questions.explanation: The correct fix is to re-import the corporate root certificate and restart the terminal. Disabling TLS verification or using a personal network breaches the information handling policy.

questions.prompt: You receive a repository permission denied error on your first clone. What should you do?

options.text: Fork the repository into your personal account
Request the role bundle for your learning role
Ask a colleague to push on your behalf
Use a personal access token from another project

questions.explanation: Repository access is granted as part of the role bundle, not as an individual repository permission. Forking client code to a personal account is a policy breach.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT an approved part of workstation setup?

options.text: Joining the HCLTech domain and completing multi-factor enrolment
Installing the pinned engineering baseline from the software portal
Upgrading the local JDK to the newest release from the public vendor site
Running the standard environment verification script

questions.explanation: Locally upgrading a toolchain outside the pinned baseline is not approved — your environment must match the build agents. Use the pinned installer if a version is missing.

questions.prompt: Where must the access request template be raised?

options.text: Through the service desk, with manager approval
In the project team chat
With the client product owner
By email to the IT director

questions.explanation: Access requests are raised through the service desk using the template for your learning role. Your manager approves the business justification and IT fulfils the request.

questions.prompt: How many bounded contexts make up the ADB platform?

options.text: Three
Four
Five
Seven

questions.explanation: There are five bounded contexts: Customer, Product, Origination, Servicing and Posting, each with one owning team and one clear contract.

questions.prompt: Why is origination described as a saga?

options.text: Because it is a single atomic database transaction
Because each step is a separate, resumable operation that can be compensated
Because it always completes synchronously in one call
Because it never pauses for manual review

questions.explanation: Origination is a saga: each step is a separate, resumable operation. When a step such as screening needs review, the case pauses with a structured reason code and can resume or compensate.

questions.prompt: Which component is the only one permitted to write to the core ledger?

options.text: The Customer context
The Origination context
The Posting service
The reporting data mart

questions.explanation: The Posting service is the only component holding ledger credentials. All movement flows through it — no other context writes to the core ledger directly.

questions.prompt: A change appears to affect the rules of two bounded contexts. What does that usually indicate?

options.text: The rule is in the wrong place and should be raised in design review
The logic should be duplicated in both contexts
The contexts should be merged immediately
The change should be implemented in the UI layer instead

questions.explanation: Business rules belong to exactly one context. If a change appears to affect two, the rule is usually in the wrong place — raise it in design review rather than duplicating logic.

questions.prompt: Which system remains the system of record for balances?

options.text: The client CRM
The core banking host
The document generation service
The screening service

questions.explanation: The core banking host remains the system of record for balances. The ADB platform orchestrates and posts through the Posting service but does not replace the host ledger.

questions.prompt: Where may Restricted data such as customer identity documents be handled?

options.text: In approved environments only, with no local copy
On your corporate laptop, if the disk is encrypted
In a personal cloud drive, if the folder is private
In a personal AI assistant, if you remove the names

questions.explanation: Restricted data is handled only in approved environments with no local copy. Encryption on a laptop does not make a local copy permissible, and personal cloud or AI tools are prohibited.

questions.prompt: You suspect you have exposed client data to an unintended recipient. What is the first thing you do?

options.text: Investigate the scope yourself before reporting
Delete the message or file to limit exposure
Stop the activity, secure the data and report within one hour
Wait to see whether anyone notices

questions.explanation: Stop the activity, secure the data you are working with, and report through the security helpline within one hour. Do not self-investigate and do not delete evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement about production database access is correct?

options.text: Direct access is allowed if you use a read-only account
Direct access is prohibited; use the approved servicing tools
Direct access is allowed during the change freeze only
Direct access is allowed with verbal approval from a teammate

questions.explanation: Direct production database access is prohibited regardless of the account's privileges. Use the approved servicing tools, which are audited.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an approved use of client data in a non-production environment?

options.text: Copying a production customer record so the test is realistic
Using synthetic data generated with the approved generator
Screenshotting production and attaching it to the ticket
Exporting a production table into a spreadsheet

questions.explanation: Test environments use synthetic or masked data only. All test data is generated with the approved synthetic data generator, never copied from production.

questions.prompt: When does the production change freeze apply?

options.text: Every Friday afternoon
From the last business day of each month
During the client's financial year end only
There is no change freeze on this programme

questions.explanation: The production change freeze runs from the last business day of each month. Releases are planned around this window.

questions.prompt: What is the correct branch naming convention?

options.text: feature/<ticket>-<slug>
yourname/<date>
<ticket>/develop
hotfix-<slug>-final-v2

questions.explanation: Branches are named feature/<ticket>-<slug>, for example feature/ADB-1421-case-retry. Names must reference the ticket so the change is traceable.

questions.prompt: How should your feature branch stay current with develop?

options.text: Merge develop into your branch daily
Rebase onto the latest develop
Never update it until the pull request is approved
Create a fresh branch from main every day

questions.explanation: Rebase your feature branch onto the latest develop and force-push with lease to your own branch. Never merge develop into the branch, and never force-push to shared branches.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended maximum size for a pull request?

options.text: 100 changed lines
400 changed lines
1,500 changed lines
There is no limit

questions.explanation: Keep pull requests under 400 changed lines. Smaller pull requests are reviewed faster, reviewed more thoroughly and are easier to revert if needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the review checklist?

options.text: Whether the author has written enough comments
Whether the new behaviour is covered by an automated test
Whether the change is large enough to be significant
Whether the author has signed off their own pull request

questions.explanation: The checklist covers correctness, tests, security and observability. A reviewer must confirm the new behaviour is covered by an automated test.

questions.prompt: Why is daily logging mandatory?

options.text: It is the client-mandated audit trail
It is used for individual performance ranking
It replaces the need for pull request reviews
It helps the team plan the social calendar

questions.explanation: Daily logging is the client-mandated audit trail for the engagement. It is not used for performance ranking and does not replace review.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a well-written unit test?

options.text: It asserts on internal fields and log output
It asserts an observable business outcome through the public interface
It depends on execution order and calls the network for realism
It covers several behaviours so the suite runs faster

questions.explanation: A unit test asserts an observable business outcome through the public interface. It never depends on network calls, sleeps, execution order or internal implementation details.

questions.prompt: What must accompany every defect fix?

options.text: A changelog entry only
A test that reproduces the original failure
A new feature branch for the next release
A written apology to the QA squad

questions.explanation: Every defect fix ships with a regression test that would have caught the original failure. A hotfix without a regression test will be re-broken by a later release.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum unit coverage expected on changed code?

options.text: 100% in every case

questions.explanation: The gate requires at least 80% unit coverage on changed code. Coverage is a floor, not a goal — boundary cases matter more than the percentage.

questions.prompt: Where is a release cut from?

options.text: The feature branch with the most recent commit
The release branch
A developer's local machine
The main branch, without review

questions.explanation: A release is cut from the release branch by the release manager. Feature branches and local machines are never used to produce a release.

questions.prompt: A failing test reveals a bug. What is the recommended debugging sequence?

options.text: Fix the symptom in production and add a test later
Reproduce with the smallest input, write a failing test, fix the cause
Disable the failing test and raise a ticket
Rewrite the module before investigating

questions.explanation: Reproduce with the smallest possible input, capture it in a failing test, then fix the cause rather than the symptom. This keeps the fix verifiable and prevents regression.

questions.prompt: What is the team's target test pyramid ratio?

options.text: 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% end-to-end
10% unit, 20% integration, 70% end-to-end
50% unit, 0% integration, 50% end-to-end
100% end-to-end so nothing is missed

questions.explanation: The target is roughly 70% unit, 20% integration and 10% end-to-end. An inverted pyramid is slow, flaky and cannot sustain a two-week release cadence.

questions.prompt: Which environment uses masked, client-owned data for acceptance?

options.text: Local
Integration
UAT
System test

questions.explanation: UAT uses masked, client-owned data and is where client acceptance happens. System test uses masked seeded data owned by the delivery team.

questions.prompt: What is the source of truth for test design?

options.text: The acceptance criteria
The developer's implementation
The previous release's test cases
The client's verbal description in stand-up

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are the source of truth. Writing tests against the implementation tends to encode the same misunderstanding the implementation contains.

questions.prompt: An exception path in the requirements has no specified behaviour. What should you do?

options.text: Skip it — it is not in scope
Raise it with the product analyst as a design gap and design a negative case
Test whatever the implementation happens to do
Mark it as blocked and move on

questions.explanation: An unspecified exception is a design gap, not a testing inconvenience. Raise it with the product analyst and design an explicit negative case — exception paths without tests are uncovered risks.

questions.prompt: At which level are domain rules and edge cases primarily tested?

options.text: Unit
System
UAT
Contract

questions.explanation: Domain rules and edge cases are tested at unit level, owned by the developer. Testers own component, contract and system level suites.

questions.prompt: How is test data created on this project?

options.text: By copying production records and anonymising the names
With the approved synthetic data generator, using a deterministic seed
By asking the client to export a sample
By hand-entering data with no record of the seed

questions.explanation: Test data is generated synthetically with the approved generator and a deterministic seed so failures are reproducible. Production data is never copied, even when anonymised by hand.

questions.prompt: What does a 'Blocked' test result mean?

options.text: The application returned an incorrect result
An environmental issue prevents execution
The tester did not have time to run the case
The case is not applicable this cycle

questions.explanation: Blocked means an environmental issue prevents execution. It is raised as an environment defect and must never be marked as failed or silently skipped.

questions.prompt: What is required before a defect can be closed?

options.text: A verbal confirmation from the developer
A passing retest and an attached evidence link
A new test case added to the suite
Client sign-off on the release

questions.explanation: A defect is closed only when the retest passes and the evidence link is attached. If the fix is incomplete, reopen the same defect rather than raising a new one.

questions.prompt: On which environment should a defect fix be retested?

options.text: Any environment that is currently available
The same environment and data as the original failure
Production, to be certain
A local environment with hand-crafted data

questions.explanation: Retest on the same environment and data as the original failure. Retesting elsewhere frequently produces a false pass and returns a real defect to the release.

questions.prompt: Why must seeded test data be cleaned up after an execution window?

options.text: To keep the environment deterministic for the next run
Because the generator licence expires daily
To reduce the size of the evidence archive
Because the client requires a weekly screenshot

questions.explanation: Leaving seeded data behind makes the next run non-deterministic and produces failures that cannot be reproduced. Cleanup keeps the environment trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between severity and priority?

options.text: Severity is urgency; priority is impact
Severity is impact; priority is urgency
They are interchangeable on this project
Severity is set by the client; priority by the tester

questions.explanation: Severity describes the impact on the system, while priority describes the urgency of fixing it. A Minor cosmetic issue on a customer-facing journey can be higher priority than a Major issue in an internal tool.

questions.prompt: A core journey is completely broken with no workaround. What severity applies?

options.text: Blocker
Critical
Major
Minor

questions.explanation: A core journey broken with no workaround is Critical. Blocker is reserved for the system being unusable or data being at risk.

questions.prompt: How should regression scope be selected?

options.text: Always run the entire suite regardless of the change
Risk-based, documented with the rationale
Only the exact journey that changed
Whichever suites ran in the previous release

questions.explanation: Regression selection is risk-based and documented. Always running the full suite is slower, and a suite that always runs eventually gets skipped under pressure.

questions.prompt: What must a release recommendation always state?

options.text: That all defects are fixed
What was tested and what was not tested
The name of the release manager
The number of test cases in the suite

questions.explanation: A release recommendation always states what was and was not tested. An unqualified 'ready' is not acceptable because it hides residual risk from the decision-maker.

questions.prompt: Which suites are always included in regression selection?

options.text: The smoke suite and the impacted journey
Only the smoke suite
Every suite in the repository
The performance suite only

questions.explanation: Always include the smoke suite and the impacted journey, then add suites sharing a service or data with the change, plus the last three release suites as a baseline.
